title: Russia introduces new laws to jail critics, but denies it holds any political prisoners
content: Every year on 30 October, the world marks the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Political Repressions. Starting in 1974, when Soviet political prisoners coordinated a collective, one-day hunger strike in defiance of their captors and to call for official recognition of their status as political prisoners, the date today carries an uncomfortable irony in Russia. People are being imprisoned there on charges that rights groups say are false, yet the authorities refuse to recognise that political prisoners exist. Memorial, one of the main groups that kept the memory of Soviet repression alive and documented today’s cases, has been liquidated in Russia and branded “extremist.” It continues its activities in exile.

title: How to justify crimes against humanity: the Kremlin method
content:
• Moscow denies its documented attacks on Ukrainian civilian infrastructure
  • Pro-Kremlin commentators deny proven war crimes against civilians
  • The “Nazi Ukraine” narrative is used once again to justify Russia’s aggression
  • Fabricated threats become fuel for escalation

    • Pro-Kremlin FIMI campaigns promoted four narratives to justify Russia’s war against Ukraine: that Russia only strikes civilian infrastructure in retaliation; that recent attacks around Kyiv ended Moscow’s supposed restraint; that Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres are part of a “fight against Nazism” in Europe; and that NATO is preparing an offensive or blockade of Kaliningrad.

    These claims ignore extensive evidence of Russian attacks on civilians and civilian infrastructure, as well as documented war crimes. They also distort the chronology and the causes of the war. By blaming Ukraine, denying Russian wrongdoing, and weaponising heavily distorted Second World War narratives, pro-Kremlin actors seek to legitimise Russia’s aggression and portray Moscow as the victim and protector of Europe.

title: Bucha denial at UNGA and Nazi narratives justifying strikes on Ukraine
content:
IN SHORT:

  • Russia uses UNGA to demand “proper investigation” into its well-documented war crimes in Bucha
  • Ukrainian officials accused of child trafficking while Russian officials are wanted by the ICC for the same crime
  • “Nazi Ukraine” narrative used to justify strikes on civilian infrastructure

    • LAST WEEK IN REVIEW

    This week’s narratives demonstrate how the Kremlin relies on familiar FIMI tactics to respond to new developments. Rather than creating entirely new narratives, pro-Kremlin actors recycle established themes and adapt them to current events. The renewed denial of the Bucha massacre is a particularly clear example. Despite extensive documentation and independent investigations, Russia continues to flood the information space with multiple, often contradictory explanations.

title: Russia’s Baltic escalation playbook: fear is part of the strategy
content:
Russia is promoting a picture of the Baltic region in which NATO is preparing to attack Russia, Baltic governments are heavily militarising, and Russian speakers face imminent persecution. Taken together, these narratives create an atmosphere of permanent crisis in which military escalation appears increasingly plausible. This allows Moscow to exert pressure even without taking overt military action – the possibility of conflict itself becomes an instrument of coercion.

In late 2025, the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) drew attention to the steady stream of Russian FIMI targeting the Baltic countries, noting that they mirror the narratives that the Kremlin used to try to justify its invasions of Ukraine. Recent Baltic intelligence assessments describe a sustained and increasingly organised Russian effort to influence the information environment in Latvia, Lithuania, and Estonia, disseminating anti-Baltic narratives through social media and coordinated cross-platform campaigns.

title: Moscow cries fraud abroad while fixing the vote at home
content:
Moscow routinely portrays elections in democratic countries as fraudulent and controlled from abroad. Yet Russia’s own parliamentary election offers no genuine political choice: the Kremlin controls the field and has eliminated even the possibility of voting against the war in Ukraine. As the war’s effects reach deeper into everyday life, growing public dissatisfaction is being kept out of the ballot box.

When post-Soviet states turn away from Russia, as Armenia or Moldova have done, Kremlin officials and aligned outlets usually blame Western interference. Yet Moscow has itself tries to influence elections through foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI), often alongside financial support for pro-Russian groups. Moldovan authorities say Russian agents spent about €200 million – nearly 1% of Moldova’s GDP – on vote-buying and disinformation during the country’s 2024 presidential election and EU referendum. Investigators later found that the sanctioned Russian organisation Evrazia had used similar tactics ahead of Armenia’s 2026 election. Moscow nevertheless portrayed EU assistance intended to counter such threats as election interference.

title: From denial to exploitation: how the Kremlin has adapted its climate disinformation
content:
In the latest wave of climate-related narratives spread by the Kremlin, climate change is a vehicle to reinforce familiar disinformation tropes: the alleged authoritarianism and hypocrisy of the EU, Europe’s supposed self-inflicted decline through sanctions against Russia, and, ultimately, the claim that Europe has no choice but to restore relations with Russia as a supplier of affordable oil and gas.

Climate change used to be a fringe topic in Kremlin propaganda. It was rarely mentioned, and when it was, it was often accompanied by absurd claims or outright denial. But as the effects of climate change become increasingly difficult to ignore (including domestically in Russia), pro-Kremlin outlets have largely stopped denying its existence. Instead, they have woven it into their disinformation ecosystem, shifting from denying the problem to discrediting proposed solutions.

title: From social media to the front line: Russia’s foreign recruitment pipeline
content: This report traces how Russia sustains its war in Ukraine by recruiting foreign nationals, many of them deceived or coerced, through a global pipeline of social media advertisements, intermediaries and disposable websites. It centres on a recent investigation by the European External Action Service (EEAS), which uncovered a coordinated digital infrastructure behind this recruitment drive.

title: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 2
content:
In official discourse, Kaliningrad is increasingly portrayed as Russia’s western fortress: resilient, patriotic, and under constant external pressure. Yet propaganda must also compete with people’s everyday experience. Rising prices, logistical disruption, security alerts and the militarisation of public life shape how residents perceive the consequences of Russia’s war. This article examines that tension between official narratives and lived reality.

The weakest point of Kremlin propaganda in Kaliningrad Oblast is the collision between the official picture of the world and the everyday economy. A person may repeat familiar formulas about ‘unfriendly countries’, ‘sanctions pressure’, and the ‘threat from the West’, while at the same time seeing that the ordinary food basket is becoming more expensive, familiar goods periodically disappear, and the region is increasingly dependent on complicated and costly logistics. In Kaliningrad, the war is felt through the price tag.

title: My home is not my castle: Kaliningrad as an address for Kremlin propaganda. Part 1
content:
Kaliningrad Oblast is a Russian semi-exclave on the Baltic Sea, separated from mainland Russia and located between Lithuania and Poland – both members of the EU and NATO. The region itself was created after the Second World War from the northern part of former East Prussia, transferred to the USSR under the Potsdam agreements in 1945. This makes Kaliningrad simultaneously a Russian territory, a former German space, a Baltic region, and Moscow’s military outpost on the border with the European Union.

Unlike most Russian regions, Kaliningrad for a long time lived not simply in a Russian reality, but in a European borderland everyday life. The local border traffic agreement between Poland and Kaliningrad Oblast significantly increased cross-border mobility. Even after it was suspended in 2016, the memory of that openness remained an important part of local identity. For Kaliningraders, Europe was not an abstract ‘hostile West’ from television, but a nearby and recognisable space just a few kilometres away.

title: Why the information space has become a minefield for EU CSDP missions and operations
content:
When Armenian voters renewed Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan’s mandate in the June 2026 parliamentary elections, they did more than choose a government. They chose closer cooperation with the European Union. That choice made them a target.

As Armenia deepened its relations with the EU, it became a frequent target of Russian Foreign Information Manipulation and Interference (FIMI). Attempts to discredit European engagements are a recurring feature relayed across social media platforms, inauthentic news websites, and foreign state-controlled outlets. FIMI has specifically targeted the EU mission in Armenia (EUMA), which was established in 2023 to monitor and support confidence-building in conflict-affected areas in the country. This pattern is telling: modern influence operations do not happen only during war time. They seek to divide partners, distort facts, shape people’s minds, manipulate their emotions, and influence their decisions.
